query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal‐element alloys (MPEAs), a sufficiently high concentration of oxidation‐active elements (notably Cr and Al) governs oxidation resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a dense, adherent passivating oxide scale that slows further oxidation and preserves material integrity in high-temperature environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous MPEA in the as-cast or homogenized state with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Increase the relative concentrations of Cr and Al (or equivalent oxidation‐active species) in one set of MPEAs compared to a baseline alloy with lower Cr/Al contents.
generation.conditions: Sustained exposure at high temperatures (e.g., 900–1100°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or controlled O₂ partial pressure) for extended durations to simulate harsh operating environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a continuous and slow‐growing oxide scale dominated by Cr₂O₃ and/or Al₂O₃ on the exposed surface.
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic preference of Cr and Al for oxidation leads to selective formation of a protective oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further diffusion of oxygen into the alloy. This passivating film slows oxidation kinetics, limits scale spallation, and thereby maintains the alloy’s structural integrity under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with increased Cr/Al will show a thinner, more adherent oxide scale with reduced growth rate and lower spallation, preserving mechanical and structural properties relative to the baseline MPEA with lower Cr/Al under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: MPEA with standard or lower concentration of Cr and Al, known from prior design to have limited oxidation resistance under severe conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature oxidizing conditions (up to ~1100°C) where protective oxide formation is thermodynamically viable. Its validity may diminish if temperature or environmental conditions favor alternative oxidation mechanisms (e.g., volatilization of oxides or scale destabilization).
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold concentrations of Cr and Al required to achieve an optimal protective oxide scale and the interplay with other alloying elements in the complex MPEA matrix remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEA samples: one with a high Cr/Al concentration and one with a lower Cr/Al concentration (baseline). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., isothermal exposure at 950°C in air) for fixed durations. Perform regular time-point analyses of the surface oxide using microscopy, spectroscopy, and mechanical testing.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness (via cross-sectional SEM or TEM)
Scale adherence/spallation events (via in situ microscopy or post-exposure mechanical testing)
Elemental composition and phase analysis of the oxide scale (via EDS or XRD)
Mechanical properties of the substrate post-oxidation (e.g., hardness, creep resistance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high Cr/Al alloy does not exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or faster oxide scale growth, greater scale spallation, and comparable or lower mechanical integrity) compared to the low Cr/Al alloy, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Cr and Al governs improved high-temperature resistance in MPEAs would be falsified.
